chapters.title: Chapter 3: Correlation, Diversification, and the Multi-Asset Risk Engine

lessons.title: Correlation in Crises: What 2008, 2020, and 2022 Taught Us About Diversification

body.text: "Crisis" is not one scenario with one correlation pattern. A liquidity crisis, a growth shock, and an inflation shock each break diversification in a genuinely different way, and a systematic desk that only has one crisis playbook, built from whichever crisis it happened to live through first, will be dangerously unprepared for the next one if it turns out to be a different type.

children.text: This course has referenced March 2020 repeatedly as the go-to example of correlation spiking during crisis. That is true, but incomplete, and incomplete in a way that matters. This lesson compares three genuinely different crises, the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, the 2020 COVID crash, and the 2022 rate-hike cycle, and shows that each one broke a different diversification assumption, for a different underlying reason.
2008: The Liquidity Crisis Where Almost Nothing Was Safe

The 2008 Global Financial Crisis was, at its core, a credit and liquidity crisis. As leveraged institutions faced margin calls and investors faced redemptions, the dominant force in markets was not a rotation from risky assets to safe ones, it was forced selling of whatever could be sold to raise cash, regardless of an asset's fundamental safety. Nifty fell by more than half, roughly 60% peak to trough, from its January 2008 highs to the October to November 2008 lows. What made 2008 unusual, and genuinely dangerous for diversification, is that even gold, this course's repeated example of a stress-period diversifier, fell sharply during the most acute phase of forced deleveraging in October 2008, before rallying strongly through 2009 as central banks around the world moved to aggressive monetary easing.

body.text: A pure liquidity crisis can temporarily break even gold's safe-haven behavior, since forced sellers raise cash from whatever is liquid enough to sell quickly, not necessarily from what is fundamentally risky. "Safe haven" is a tendency observed across most crises, not a guarantee that holds in every single one.

children.text: 2020: The Growth Shock Where Diversification Actually Worked

The COVID crash was a demand and growth shock, met almost immediately with a massive, coordinated monetary and fiscal response: the RBI and central banks globally cut rates sharply, and governments deployed large fiscal packages. In this environment, the classic diversification playbook worked close to textbook. As shown in Chapter 1's opening chart, Nifty fell close to 38% while G-Secs rallied on rate-cut expectations and gold held up and later rallied strongly. This is the crisis pattern most "buy gold and bonds for protection" advice implicitly assumes, and it is worth being explicit that this pattern is not universal, it is what happens specifically when the shock is a growth shock met with easing, not every kind of crisis.
2022: The Inflation Shock That Broke the 60/40 Playbook

2022 broke a different assumption entirely. Inflation surged globally, and the RBI, alongside central banks worldwide, hiked rates aggressively, the RBI's repo rate rising from 4% to 6.5% across the cycle. This was a shock to the discount rate itself, and a rise in the discount rate hurts equities, since future earnings are worth less discounted at a higher rate, and hurts bonds simultaneously, since bond prices fall directly as yields rise, the duration mechanics covered in Chapter 2. Equities and bonds, which had been reliably negatively correlated for most investors' working memory, moved together through 2022. This is precisely the assumption Chapter 6's risk parity approach depends on, and precisely the scenario where it is most exposed.

body.title: Illustrative Equity-Bond Rolling Correlation During Three Crises

body.text: The correlation values in this chart and the table above are illustrative, built to reflect the well-documented direction of each period, not precise computed historical series. Treat them as directionally instructive characterizations of each crisis type.

The type of shock, not just its severity, determines which correlations spike and which decouple. A liquidity crisis threatens almost everything, including gold. A growth shock met with easing rewards the classic stocks-and-bonds hedge. An inflation shock, met with tightening, breaks that same hedge. Knowing which kind of shock you are in matters as much as knowing a shock is happening at all.

children.text: What This Means for Building a Systematic Multi-Asset System

Lesson 2's correlation breakdown signal, a widening gap between short-window and long-window correlation, tells a desk that something has changed. It does not, by itself, tell the desk what kind of shock is unfolding or which of its diversifiers are still likely to work. That requires layering in context: is this primarily a liquidity event, a growth shock, or an inflation shock? This is not a question correlation data alone answers, and it is exactly why this course does not stop at correlation. Chapter 4 builds trend signals that can help identify which kind of regime is underway, and Chapter 9's risk management explicitly assumes that any given crisis playbook can fail if the next crisis turns out to be a different type than the one the playbook was built for.

body.title: The Playbook Built From One Crisis
body.scenario: A systematic desk built its entire risk-management framework in 2021, using 2020's COVID crash as its defining crisis template: when equities fall sharply, add to bonds and gold, since both reliably rallied during that crisis. In the first half of 2022, as inflation surged and the RBI began hiking rates, the desk's Nifty futures position lost money as expected, but its G-Sec position, added specifically as a hedge, lost money too.
body.prompt: What went wrong with the desk's risk-management framework, and how should it be redesigned given what this lesson covered?
body.modelAnswer: The desk's framework generalized a single crisis's correlation pattern, 2020's negative equity-bond correlation, into a universal rule, treating bonds as an automatic hedge against any equity drawdown. 2022 was a different type of shock, an inflation shock met with aggressive tightening, which raises the discount rate and hurts equities and bonds simultaneously through completely different mechanisms, earnings discounting for equities, direct yield-driven price declines for bonds. The framework needed to be redesigned around shock type, not just "equities down, add bonds and gold," incorporating some read on whether the current stress looks more like a liquidity event, a growth shock, or an inflation shock, and adjusting which diversifiers it actually expects to work accordingly, rather than assuming any one crisis's playbook applies universally.

body.title: Identifying the 2022 Mechanism
body.question: Why did equities and bonds move together, rather than in opposite directions, during the 2022 rate-hike cycle?
options: Because gold and bonds are always positively correlated with equities
Because the shock was a rise in the discount rate itself, which hurts equity valuations and bond prices through separate but simultaneous mechanisms
Because the RBI stopped intervening in fixed income markets that year
Because Nifty and G-Sec futures share the same exchange and clearing infrastructure
body.explanation: 2022's inflation shock led to aggressive rate hikes, which raised the discount rate applied to future equity earnings, hurting equity valuations, while simultaneously pushing bond yields up and bond prices down directly through duration mechanics. Both asset classes were hit by the same underlying driver, a rising discount rate, through two different transmission channels, which is why their usual negative correlation broke down.

body.title: Before Trusting a Diversifier in the Next Crisis, Ask
steps: What type of shock produced my portfolio's historical crisis data: a liquidity crisis, a growth shock, or an inflation shock?
Would this specific diversifier have worked in all three of 2008, 2020, and 2022, or only in the one my backtest happens to cover?
Is the current stress event driven by forced selling and deleveraging, by a demand collapse, or by rising rates and inflation?
Does my risk framework have more than one crisis playbook, or does it assume every future crisis looks like the last one it was built around?
Have I checked whether my "safe haven" assets have ever failed to behave as expected, and under what conditions that happened?

points: 2008 was a liquidity crisis where forced deleveraging temporarily broke even gold's safe-haven behavior, before it rallied strongly once easing began
2020 was a growth shock met with aggressive easing, the closest thing to a textbook case of stocks, bonds, and gold behaving exactly as classic diversification theory predicts
2022 was an inflation shock met with tightening, which raised the discount rate and hurt equities and bonds simultaneously, flipping their usual negative correlation positive
The type of underlying shock, not just its severity, determines which correlations spike and which assets decouple
Correlation breakdown, from Lesson 2, signals that something has changed, but does not by itself identify which kind of shock is unfolding or which diversifiers will still work

A systematic risk framework built from a single historical crisis risks generalizing that crisis's specific correlation pattern into a universal rule that fails the next time the shock is a different type
